# Task: describe the shell command `convert` for downstream tools

## Objective

Produce a machine-readable description of the shell command `convert` so that other programs can
understand it without ever running it themselves. One such program is PaSh, a tool that rewrites shell
scripts to run faster. Programs like PaSh need two things about a command: its **argument syntax**
(the options it accepts, the type of each option's argument, and the types of its operands), and how a
given invocation **behaves** with respect to its inputs and outputs.

The command's binary is at `/usr/bin/convert`. Its manual page is at `/usr/share/man/man1/convert-im6.q16.1.gz`.

## Deliverable

Write the following into the `output/` directory of this folder.

1. **The syntax description**, `output/convert.py`: the options the command accepts, the type of
   argument each option takes, and the types of its operands. The format is specified in
   [formats/syntax_description.md](formats/syntax_description.md).

2. **The behaviour annotation**, in the form PaSh consumes, under `output/pash/`:
   - `convert.json`, PaSh's table of the command's flags and options;
   - `InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>.py`, a Python class that, given a parsed invocation, decides
     which arguments are inputs, which are outputs, and whether standard input and output are used;
   - `ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>.py`, a Python class that, given a parsed invocation,
     decides whether and how its work can be split across parallel copies of the command.

   `<Command>` is the command's name with its first letter capitalised. The format of all three files
   is specified in [formats/pash_annotation.md](formats/pash_annotation.md).

## Examples of finished output

The `samples/` directory holds the complete set for four other commands:

| Command | Syntax description | PaSh annotation |
|---|---|---|
| `tee`  | [samples/tee/tee.py](samples/tee/tee.py)     | [samples/tee/pash/](samples/tee/pash/)   |
| `uniq` | [samples/uniq/uniq.py](samples/uniq/uniq.py) | [samples/uniq/pash/](samples/uniq/pash/) |
| `grep` | [samples/grep/grep.py](samples/grep/grep.py) | [samples/grep/pash/](samples/grep/pash/) |
| `rm`   | [samples/rm/rm.py](samples/rm/rm.py)         | [samples/rm/pash/](samples/rm/pash/)     |

## What you may not use

Do not search the web or read anything online: no search engines, no websites, no code repositories.
Work from what is on this machine. Programs that need the network to do their job, such as a package
installer, may still use it.

## Scope

The command to describe in this session is `convert`. Please generate a correct specification
without my intervention, and be certain to test the binary against the specification you generate.
When the files are written, report what you did and anything you are unsure about.

This file states the command's argument syntax: the options it accepts, the type of argument each

from caruca.ir.syntax import *

<command>_syntax_spec: list[SyntaxSpecification] = [

]

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Format: the behaviour annotation, as PaSh consumes it

PaSh describes a command with three files. Together they let PaSh parse an invocation of the command,
work out which of its arguments are inputs and outputs, and decide whether the invocation's work can be
split across parallel copies. The files live in the `pash_annotations` Python package (the module
paths below are that package's), and the samples under `samples/*/pash/` are copied from it unchanged.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<command>.json` | the parser table: the command's flags and options, and the type of each option's argument |
| `InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, marks which operands and option arguments are read, which are written, and whether standard input and standard output are used |
| `ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, lists the ways its work may be split and recombined; when the file is absent, PaSh treats the command as not parallelisable |

`<Command>` is the command's name with its first letter capitalised (`grep` → `Grep`).

## 1. The parser table, `<command>.json`

```json
{
    "flag": [
        ["-c", "--count"],
        ["-D"],
        "-f"
    ],
    "option": [
        ["-e", "PATTERNS"],
        ["--regexp", "PATTERNS"],
        ["-f", "--file", ["FILE", "CONFIG_INPUT"]]
    ]
}
```

- `flag` lists the options that take no argument. Each entry is a list of the spellings of one flag;
  the first spelling is the one the parser reports. A bare string is accepted as a one-spelling entry.
- `option` lists the options that take an argument. Each entry is one or more spellings followed by
  the argument's type name. The type name is free text taken from the manual (`NUM`, `WHEN`, `MODE`),
  except that a file argument is written as a two-element list, `["FILE", <access>]`, where `FILE`,
  `DIR` or `DIRECTORY` marks it as a path and `<access>` is one of the access kinds in section 4.
- Two spellings of the same option may be listed as separate entries (grep's `-e` and `--regexp`) or in
  one entry (`-f`, `--file`).

PaSh's parser reads an invocation left to right: words found in `flag` or `option` are collected, with
an option consuming the following word as its argument; a word of the form `-abc` whose letters are all
flags is split into them; the first word that is none of these starts the operand list.

## 2. The input/output class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.InputOutputInfoGenerator_Interface import InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface


class InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>(InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

The class defines one method, `generate_info`. PaSh constructs the object with the parsed invocation,
calls `generate_info`, and reads the result. Before `generate_info` runs, every operand is already
marked as a streaming input and option arguments are already typed from the parser table; the method
changes what differs for this command and this invocation.

**Inspecting the invocation** (inherited):

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q", "-c"])` | whether any of the named flags or options is present |
| `self.get_flag_option_list_filtered_with([...])` | the present ones among those named |
| `self.get_operand_list_length()` | the number of operands |
| `self.get_first_operand_name_as_string()` | the first operand's text |
| `self.does_first_operand_start_with(s)`, `self.does_first_operand_contain(s)` | tests on that text |
| `self.cmd_inv.flag_option_list`, `self.cmd_inv.operand_list` | the parsed lists themselves |

**Declaring inputs and outputs** (inherited):

| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdin()` | standard input is read even though no operand names it |
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdout()` | standard output is written |
| `self.if_no_operands_given_stdin_implicitly_used()` | the first, only when there are no operands |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_inputs()` | every operand is a file read as a stream (the default) |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_outputs()` | every operand is a file written as a stream |
| `self.all_operands_are_other_inputs()` / `..._other_outputs()` | every operand is a file read, or written, in some non-streaming way |
| `self.all_but_last_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._other_input()` | the last operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.all_but_first_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._streaming_output()` / `..._other_input()` | the first operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.only_last_operand_is_stream_output()` / `..._other_output()` | the last operand alone is an output |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_string()` | the first operand is not a file but a value, such as a pattern |
| `self.set_all_operands_as_config_arg_type_string()` | no operand is a file |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_filename_or_std_descriptor()` | the first operand is a file read as configuration rather than as a stream |

## 3. The parallelizability class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator_Interface import ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface


class ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>(ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

Again one method, `generate_info`, with the same inspection calls as above. It appends zero or more
**parallelizers** to a list. A parallelizer is a splitter, a mapper and an aggregator: how the input is
divided, what runs on each part, and how the parts' outputs are recombined. Appending nothing means the
invocation is not parallelised.

**Splitters:** `indiv_files` (each input file is its own part), `consec_chunks` (the input is cut into
consecutive pieces), `round_robin` (lines are dealt out to parts in turn).

**Mappers:** by default the same command runs on each part (`seq`). A custom mapper is named with
`make_mapper_spec_custom(name, is_implemented=...)` from
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.MapperSpec`.

**Aggregators:** `conc` (concatenate the parts' outputs in order; the default), `adj_lines_merge`
(merge the boundary lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_seq` (run the command itself over the boundary
lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_func` (a named function over the boundary lines), and custom
2-ary or n-ary functions. The `make_aggregator_spec_*` constructors live in
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.AggregatorSpec`; the ones that take
a function name also take `is_implemented`, and a name beginning `PLACEHOLDER:` marks a function PaSh
does not yet provide.

**Appending a parallelizer**, in two forms:

- The inherited one-call shortcuts, named `append_to_parallelizer_list_<splitter>_seq_<aggregator>`
  with splitter in `if`, `cc`, `rr` and aggregator in `conc`, `adjm`, `adjs`, `adjf`; the `adjf` ones
  take `(string_repr_func, is_implemented)`. Examples: `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_cc_seq_conc()`,
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_rr_seq_adjs()`.
- Building one explicitly with `make_parallelizer_consec_chunks(...)`,
  `make_parallelizer_round_robin(...)` or `make_parallelizer_indiv_files(...)` from
  `pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.Parallelizer`, each taking
  optional `mapper_spec`, `aggregator_spec` and `info_splitter_mapper` (an
  `AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper` value: `NO_ADD_INPUT`, `LINE_NUM_OFFSET`, `BYTE_OFFSET`,
  `LINE_NUM_AND_BYTE_OFFSET`, for mappers that need to know where their part began), then
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer)`.

`self.set_commutative()` records that the parts' outputs may be recombined in any order.

## 4. Access kinds

Used in the parser table's file-argument entries and behind the input/output calls above:

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `STREAM_INPUT` | a file read as the data stream the command processes |
| `CONFIG_INPUT` | a file read for configuration, such as a pattern file |
| `CONTAINER_FOR_INPUT` | a file that lists the real input files |
| `EXCLUDES_FROM_INPUT` | a file that lists what to leave out |
| `OTHER_INPUT` | read in some other way |
| `STREAM_OUTPUT` | a file written as the output stream |
| `OTHER_OUTPUT` | written, created or removed in some other way |

from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.InputOutputInfoGenerator_Interface import InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface
from pash_annotations.datatypes.BasicDatatypes import Operand


class InputOutputInfoGeneratorGrep(InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface):

    # list_of_all_flags = ["-V", "--help", "-E", "-F", "-G", "-P", "-i", "--no-ignore-case", "-v", "-w",
    #                      "-x", "-y", "-c", "-L", "-l", "-o", "-q", "-s", "-b", "-H", "-h", "-n", "-T", "-Z",
    #                      "--no-group-separator", "-a", "-I", "-r", "-R", "--line-buffered", "-U", "-z"]
    # list_of_all_options = ["-e", "-f", "--color", "-m", "--label", "-A", "-B", "-C", "--group-separator",
    #                        "--binary-files", "-D", "-d", "--exclude", "--exclude-from", "--exclude-dir", "--include"]

    # Which ones do affect input/output?
    # -f affects input
    # -r actually does not really affect both since files and directories are both identified by their name
    # for now, we ignore --exclude, --exclude-from, --exclude-dir, and --include and, thus, over-approximate
    # for now, we ignore -D/-d with actions

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        # --help and --version overrules -q (and no actual result returned) but we assume no help/version
        if not self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q"]):
            self.set_implicit_use_of_stdout()
        # case analysis how script is provided
        if self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-e", "-f"]):
            if self.get_operand_list_length() == 0:
                self.set_implicit_use_of_stdin()
            else:
                self.all_operands_are_streaming_inputs() # this is true also if empty
        else:
            self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_string()
            if self.get_operand_list_length() == 1:
                self.set_implicit_use_of_stdin()
            else:
                self.all_but_first_operand_is_streaming_input()

from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator_Interface import ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.Parallelizer import \
    AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper, make_parallelizer_round_robin, make_parallelizer_consec_chunks
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.MapperSpec import make_mapper_spec_custom
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.AggregatorSpec import \
    make_aggregator_spec_custom_2_ary_from_string_representation


class ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorGrep(ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface):

    # list_of_all_flags = ["-V", "--help", "-E", "-F", "-G", "-P", "-i", "--no-ignore-case", "-v", "-w",
    #                      "-x", "-y", "-c", "-L", "-l", "-o", "-q", "-s", "-b", "-H", "-h", "-n", "-T", "-Z",
    #                      "--no-group-separator", "-a", "-I", "-r", "-R", "--line-buffered", "-U", "-z"]
    # list_of_all_options = ["-e", "-f", "--color", "-m", "--label", "-A", "-B", "-C", "--group-separator",
    #                        "--binary-files", "-D", "-d", "--exclude", "--exclude-from", "--exclude-dir", "--include"]

    # Which ones do affect parallelizability?
    # -c, -L, -l, -b, -n;
    # by checking, -L and -l overrule -c overrule -b and -n; output of -n always precedes output of -b
    # assumption: RR not over file boundaries
    # and -A, -B, and -C but we do not parallelize within file boundaries since they require context
    # for -q, the input is not read further after some condition is met, so we do not parallelize at all
    # for -m, we only do IF

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        if not self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q"]):
            # # for indiv files
            # self.append_to_parallelizer_list_if_seq_conc()
            # rest for round-robin
            mapper_spec = None
            aggregator_spec = None
            add_info_from_splitter = None
            # CA to decide which mapper or aggregator, parallelizer added after CA
            if not self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-A", "-B", "-C", "-m"]):
                if self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-L", "-l"]):
                    # the output for both options is either empty or the filename (same for both if so)
                    # for "-l": if there was a match in one part, the filename will propagate; if not, not
                    # for "-L": if there was no match in one part, the filename will propagate; it not, not
                    aggregator_spec = make_aggregator_spec_custom_2_ary_from_string_representation(cmd_inv_as_str='PLACEHOLDER:merge_keeping_longer_output',
                                                                                       is_implemented=False)
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-c"]):
                    aggregator_spec = make_aggregator_spec_custom_2_ary_from_string_representation(cmd_inv_as_str='PLACEHOLDER:sum_indiv_results_up',
                                                                                       is_implemented=False)
                    # cat input1 input2 | paste -s -d + - | bc
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-n"]) and self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-b"]):
                    mapper_spec = make_mapper_spec_custom('PLACEHOLDER:grep_add_line_number_and_byte_offset',
                                                                     is_implemented=False)
                    add_info_from_splitter=AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper.LINE_NUM_AND_BYTE_OFFSET
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-n"]):
                    mapper_spec = make_mapper_spec_custom('PLACEHOLDER:grep_add_line_number_offset',
                                                                     is_implemented=False)
                    add_info_from_splitter=AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper.LINE_NUM_OFFSET
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-b"]):
                    mapper_spec = make_mapper_spec_custom('PLACEHOLDER:grep_add_byte_offset',
                                                                     is_implemented=False)
                    add_info_from_splitter = AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper.BYTE_OFFSET
                else:   # none of the above affecting flags
                    pass    #just keep mapper and aggregator None and thus add RR_SEQ_CONC
            # we exploit that mapper_spec becomes seq and aggregator_spec becomes conc if given None
            # check can be removed once all are implemented! (exploits short-circuiting)
            # TODO: we should be able to remove the `is_implemented`-check as it is checked later
            if (mapper_spec is None or mapper_spec.is_implemented) and \
                    (aggregator_spec is None or aggregator_spec.is_implemented):
                parallelizer_cc = make_parallelizer_consec_chunks(mapper_spec=mapper_spec,
                                                                  aggregator_spec=aggregator_spec,
                                                                  info_splitter_mapper=add_info_from_splitter)
                self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer_cc)
                parallelizer_rr = make_parallelizer_round_robin(mapper_spec=mapper_spec,
                                                                 aggregator_spec=aggregator_spec,
                                                                 info_splitter_mapper=add_info_from_splitter)
                self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer_rr)

# Format: the behaviour annotation, as PaSh consumes it

PaSh describes a command with three files. Together they let PaSh parse an invocation of the command,
work out which of its arguments are inputs and outputs, and decide whether the invocation's work can be
split across parallel copies. The files live in the `pash_annotations` Python package (the module
paths below are that package's), and the samples under `samples/*/pash/` are copied from it unchanged.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `<command>.json` | the parser table: the command's flags and options, and the type of each option's argument |
| `InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, marks which operands and option arguments are read, which are written, and whether standard input and standard output are used |
| `ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>.py` | a class that, given a parsed invocation, lists the ways its work may be split and recombined; when the file is absent, PaSh treats the command as not parallelisable |

`<Command>` is the command's name with its first letter capitalised (`grep` → `Grep`).

## 1. The parser table, `<command>.json`

```json
{
    "flag": [
        ["-c", "--count"],
        ["-D"],
        "-f"
    ],
    "option": [
        ["-e", "PATTERNS"],
        ["--regexp", "PATTERNS"],
        ["-f", "--file", ["FILE", "CONFIG_INPUT"]]
    ]
}
```

- `flag` lists the options that take no argument. Each entry is a list of the spellings of one flag;
  the first spelling is the one the parser reports. A bare string is accepted as a one-spelling entry.
- `option` lists the options that take an argument. Each entry is one or more spellings followed by
  the argument's type name. The type name is free text taken from the manual (`NUM`, `WHEN`, `MODE`),
  except that a file argument is written as a two-element list, `["FILE", <access>]`, where `FILE`,
  `DIR` or `DIRECTORY` marks it as a path and `<access>` is one of the access kinds in section 4.
- Two spellings of the same option may be listed as separate entries (grep's `-e` and `--regexp`) or in
  one entry (`-f`, `--file`).

PaSh's parser reads an invocation left to right: words found in `flag` or `option` are collected, with
an option consuming the following word as its argument; a word of the form `-abc` whose letters are all
flags is split into them; the first word that is none of these starts the operand list.

## 2. The input/output class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.InputOutputInfoGenerator_Interface import InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface


class InputOutputInfoGenerator<Command>(InputOutputInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

The class defines one method, `generate_info`. PaSh constructs the object with the parsed invocation,
calls `generate_info`, and reads the result. Before `generate_info` runs, every operand is already
marked as a streaming input and option arguments are already typed from the parser table; the method
changes what differs for this command and this invocation.

**Inspecting the invocation** (inherited):

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q", "-c"])` | whether any of the named flags or options is present |
| `self.get_flag_option_list_filtered_with([...])` | the present ones among those named |
| `self.get_operand_list_length()` | the number of operands |
| `self.get_first_operand_name_as_string()` | the first operand's text |
| `self.does_first_operand_start_with(s)`, `self.does_first_operand_contain(s)` | tests on that text |
| `self.cmd_inv.flag_option_list`, `self.cmd_inv.operand_list` | the parsed lists themselves |

**Declaring inputs and outputs** (inherited):

| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdin()` | standard input is read even though no operand names it |
| `self.set_implicit_use_of_stdout()` | standard output is written |
| `self.if_no_operands_given_stdin_implicitly_used()` | the first, only when there are no operands |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_inputs()` | every operand is a file read as a stream (the default) |
| `self.all_operands_are_streaming_outputs()` | every operand is a file written as a stream |
| `self.all_operands_are_other_inputs()` / `..._other_outputs()` | every operand is a file read, or written, in some non-streaming way |
| `self.all_but_last_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._other_input()` | the last operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.all_but_first_operand_is_streaming_input()` / `..._streaming_output()` / `..._other_input()` | the first operand is left for a separate call |
| `self.only_last_operand_is_stream_output()` / `..._other_output()` | the last operand alone is an output |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_string()` | the first operand is not a file but a value, such as a pattern |
| `self.set_all_operands_as_config_arg_type_string()` | no operand is a file |
| `self.set_first_operand_as_config_arg_type_filename_or_std_descriptor()` | the first operand is a file read as configuration rather than as a stream |

## 3. The parallelizability class

```python
from pash_annotations.annotation_generation.annotation_generators.ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator_Interface import ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface


class ParallelizabilityInfoGenerator<Command>(ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface):

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        ...
```

Again one method, `generate_info`, with the same inspection calls as above. It appends zero or more
**parallelizers** to a list. A parallelizer is a splitter, a mapper and an aggregator: how the input is
divided, what runs on each part, and how the parts' outputs are recombined. Appending nothing means the
invocation is not parallelised.

**Splitters:** `indiv_files` (each input file is its own part), `consec_chunks` (the input is cut into
consecutive pieces), `round_robin` (lines are dealt out to parts in turn).

**Mappers:** by default the same command runs on each part (`seq`). A custom mapper is named with
`make_mapper_spec_custom(name, is_implemented=...)` from
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.MapperSpec`.

**Aggregators:** `conc` (concatenate the parts' outputs in order; the default), `adj_lines_merge`
(merge the boundary lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_seq` (run the command itself over the boundary
lines of adjacent parts), `adj_lines_func` (a named function over the boundary lines), and custom
2-ary or n-ary functions. The `make_aggregator_spec_*` constructors live in
`pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.AggregatorSpec`; the ones that take
a function name also take `is_implemented`, and a name beginning `PLACEHOLDER:` marks a function PaSh
does not yet provide.

**Appending a parallelizer**, in two forms:

- The inherited one-call shortcuts, named `append_to_parallelizer_list_<splitter>_seq_<aggregator>`
  with splitter in `if`, `cc`, `rr` and aggregator in `conc`, `adjm`, `adjs`, `adjf`; the `adjf` ones
  take `(string_repr_func, is_implemented)`. Examples: `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_cc_seq_conc()`,
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list_rr_seq_adjs()`.
- Building one explicitly with `make_parallelizer_consec_chunks(...)`,
  `make_parallelizer_round_robin(...)` or `make_parallelizer_indiv_files(...)` from
  `pash_annotations.annotation_generation.datatypes.parallelizability.Parallelizer`, each taking
  optional `mapper_spec`, `aggregator_spec` and `info_splitter_mapper` (an
  `AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper` value: `NO_ADD_INPUT`, `LINE_NUM_OFFSET`, `BYTE_OFFSET`,
  `LINE_NUM_AND_BYTE_OFFSET`, for mappers that need to know where their part began), then
  `self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer)`.

`self.set_commutative()` records that the parts' outputs may be recombined in any order.

## 4. Access kinds

Used in the parser table's file-argument entries and behind the input/output calls above:

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `STREAM_INPUT` | a file read as the data stream the command processes |
| `CONFIG_INPUT` | a file read for configuration, such as a pattern file |
| `CONTAINER_FOR_INPUT` | a file that lists the real input files |
| `EXCLUDES_FROM_INPUT` | a file that lists what to leave out |
| `OTHER_INPUT` | read in some other way |
| `STREAM_OUTPUT` | a file written as the output stream |
| `OTHER_OUTPUT` | written, created or removed in some other way |

class ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorGrep(ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorInterface):

    #                      "-x", "-y", "-c", "-L", "-l", "-o", "-q", "-s", "-b", "-H", "-h", "-n", "-T", "-Z",
    #                      "--no-group-separator", "-a", "-I", "-r", "-R", "--line-buffered", "-U", "-z"]
    # list_of_all_options = ["-e", "-f", "--color", "-m", "--label", "-A", "-B", "-C", "--group-separator",
    #                        "--binary-files", "-D", "-d", "--exclude", "--exclude-from", "--exclude-dir", "--include"]

    # Which ones do affect parallelizability?
    # -c, -L, -l, -b, -n;
    # by checking, -L and -l overrule -c overrule -b and -n; output of -n always precedes output of -b
    # assumption: RR not over file boundaries
    # and -A, -B, and -C but we do not parallelize within file boundaries since they require context
    # for -q, the input is not read further after some condition is met, so we do not parallelize at all
    # for -m, we only do IF

    def generate_info(self) -> None:
        if not self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-q"]):
            # # for indiv files
            # self.append_to_parallelizer_list_if_seq_conc()
            # rest for round-robin
            mapper_spec = None
            aggregator_spec = None
            add_info_from_splitter = None
            # CA to decide which mapper or aggregator, parallelizer added after CA
            if not self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-A", "-B", "-C", "-m"]):
                if self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-L", "-l"]):
                    # the output for both options is either empty or the filename (same for both if so)
                    # for "-l": if there was a match in one part, the filename will propagate; if not, not
                    # for "-L": if there was no match in one part, the filename will propagate; it not, not
                    aggregator_spec = make_aggregator_spec_custom_2_ary_from_string_representation(cmd_inv_as_str='PLACEHOLDER:merge_keeping_longer_output',
                                                                                       is_implemented=False)
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-c"]):
                    aggregator_spec = make_aggregator_spec_custom_2_ary_from_string_representation(cmd_inv_as_str='PLACEHOLDER:sum_indiv_results_up',
                                                                                       is_implemented=False)
                    # cat input1 input2 | paste -s -d + - | bc
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-n"]) and self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-b"]):
                    mapper_spec = make_mapper_spec_custom('PLACEHOLDER:grep_add_line_number_and_byte_offset',
                                                                     is_implemented=False)
                    add_info_from_splitter=AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper.LINE_NUM_AND_BYTE_OFFSET
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-n"]):
                    mapper_spec = make_mapper_spec_custom('PLACEHOLDER:grep_add_line_number_offset',
                                                                     is_implemented=False)
                    add_info_from_splitter=AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper.LINE_NUM_OFFSET
                elif self.does_flag_option_list_contain_at_least_one_of(["-b"]):
                    mapper_spec = make_mapper_spec_custom('PLACEHOLDER:grep_add_byte_offset',
                                                                     is_implemented=False)
                    add_info_from_splitter = AdditionalInfoSplitterToMapper.BYTE_OFFSET
                else:   # none of the above affecting flags
                    pass    #just keep mapper and aggregator None and thus add RR_SEQ_CONC
            # we exploit that mapper_spec becomes seq and aggregator_spec becomes conc if given None
            # check can be removed once all are implemented! (exploits short-circuiting)
            # TODO: we should be able to remove the `is_implemented`-check as it is checked later
            if (mapper_spec is None or mapper_spec.is_implemented) and \
                    (aggregator_spec is None or aggregator_spec.is_implemented):
                parallelizer_cc = make_parallelizer_consec_chunks(mapper_spec=mapper_spec,
                                                                  aggregator_spec=aggregator_spec,
                                                                  info_splitter_mapper=add_info_from_splitter)
                self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer_cc)
                parallelizer_rr = make_parallelizer_round_robin(mapper_spec=mapper_spec,
                                                                 aggregator_spec=aggregator_spec,
                                                                 info_splitter_mapper=add_info_from_splitter)
                self.append_to_parallelizer_list(parallelizer_rr)

The four deliverables are written and tested against the binary.

**What I did**

- Extracted the option table from the man page and from the binary's own `-help` output, then probed every candidate option name found in the ImageMagick library strings. The binary accepts 261 option names. The man page's `-connected-component` is a typo (only `-connected-components` works), and the binary accepts eleven undocumented options (`-average`, `-cache`, `-concurrent`, `-duration`, `-gaussian`, `-linewidth`, `-maximum`, `-minimum`, `-noop`, `-recolor`, `-metric`), which I included.
- Measured how many arguments each option takes in both `-` and `+` forms by checking whether a trailing output filename got swallowed. Eleven `-` options and three `+` options take two arguments. Many `+` forms take none where the `-` form takes one.
- Pulled the value catalogues from `convert -list` to fill in `Selection` choices for the enumerated options (colorspace, compose, filter, gravity, and so on).
- Verified behaviour: `-` or `fmt:-` as an input reads stdin, as the last operand writes stdout; `-write` produces a side output; `-identify`, `-print`, `-verbose`, `-list`, `-help`, `-version` print to stdout; options are never written with `=`; `@file` lists are blocked by this machine's security policy.

**Files in `output/`**

- `convert.py`: one syntax, 426 option nodes, operands `Path(ZERO_OR_MORE, dash_as_stdin)` followed by `Path(EXACTLY_ONE)` for the output file.
- `pash/convert.json`: 219 flag entries and 207 option entries, with file arguments typed as CONFIG_INPUT, OTHER_INPUT, or OTHER_OUTPUT.
- `pash/InputOutputInfoGeneratorConvert.py`: all but the last operand are other inputs, the last is an other output, with stdin and stdout detection for `-` operands, stdout-printing options, and `-write png:-`.
- `pash/ParallelizabilityInfoGeneratorConvert.py`: appends nothing, since image conversion is not splittable.

**Testing**

I built stub `caruca.ir.syntax` and PaSh interface modules, imported the spec, confirmed the `.py` and `.json` list the same spellings, and ran every spelling through the real binary with a valid value plus one extra token to confirm acceptance and argument count. All 522 spellings passed. The IO generator was exercised on nine invocations under both possible parser readings.

**Things I am unsure about**

- Two-argument options cannot be expressed in either format. I describe the first argument and note the second in a comment; PaSh will see the second word as an operand.
- `(`, `)`, and pseudo-images such as `xc:red` or `rose:` end up marked as input files, since the interface has no per-operand marking.
- The PaSh operand accessor names are unknown to me, so the generator reads operand text through a small attribute fallback that ends in `str()`.
- Whether `Selection` matching is case-insensitive is unknown; the binary accepts any case, and I listed the names as `-list` prints them.
